name: Oracle Database
tagline: The enterprise heavyweight: RAC, Data Guard and a converged engine for SQL, JSON, graph and vectors.
description: Oracle Database is the commercial RDBMS that most banks, telcos and ERP estates are built on. It packs features competitors still split across products: Real Application Clusters for shared-disk scale-out, Data Guard for disaster recovery, partitioning, an in-memory column store and Flashback queries. The 26ai line (shipped as release update 23.26.0 in October 2025) is explicitly converged, putting JSON Relational Duality, SQL property graphs, AI Vector Search and Iceberg tables in one engine, and 23ai systems move to it by patching rather than upgrading. The catch is cost and lock-in: most headline capabilities are paid options on top of Enterprise Edition, and licence compliance is a real operational discipline.

pricing.notes: Licensed per processor or named user; RAC, Partitioning, In-Memory, Active Data Guard etc. are extra-cost options. A resource-capped Oracle AI Database Free edition exists.

scale.notes: Scale-out via RAC (shared disk) or Globally Distributed Database (sharding, Raft replication); multi-region writes via GoldenGate. All are paid options.

strengths: RAC lets several servers write to one database for HA without sharding the schema
Data Guard and Active Data Guard give mature, well-understood DR with readable standbys
Converged engine: JSON Duality views, SQL property graphs and AI Vector Search beside relational tables
Flashback query/table/database makes recovering from bad writes a SQL statement, not a restore
Optimizer, partitioning and parallel query handle very large mixed OLTP and reporting workloads
Runs natively inside AWS, Azure and Google Cloud data centres via Oracle Database@ offerings
weaknesses: Expensive: core HA, scale and performance features are separately licensed options
Licensing rules (virtualisation, cloud vCPU counting) are complex and audit-prone
Operational depth required: patching, RMAN, ASM and RAC need specialist DBAs
Proprietary PL/SQL and features make migration away costly
useCases: Packaged ERP back ends (Oracle E-Business Suite, JD Edwards, PeopleSoft)
Mixed OLTP plus in-database analytics and vector search
Consolidating many schemas onto Exadata with multitenant PDBs
notIdealFor: Teams without DBA capacity for patching and licence management
Simple CRUD apps that PostgreSQL or MySQL serve fine
